entities.name: William V, Prince of Orange
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
William V (1748–1806), Prince of Orange and Nassau, served as the last Stadtholder of the Dutch Republic from 1751 until its collapse in 1795. Born into a long lineage of stadtholders, his early life was shaped by the regency of his mother, Anne, Princess Royal, and later by Duke Louis Ernest of Brunswick-Lüneburg, who exerted considerable influence over his political and military decisions. His reign was characterized by increasing internal political strife between the staunchly Orangeist faction and the Patriot movement, which sought to reform the decentralized, aristocratic structure of the Republic and align it with Enlightenment ideals and revolutionary France.

The core of William V's rule was marked by a gradual weakening of the Dutch Republic's international standing and military capabilities, particularly evident during the disastrous Fourth Anglo-Dutch War (1780–1784), which severely damaged the Republic's maritime trade and prestige. His perceived indecisiveness and reliance on Brunswick-Lüneburg fueled the Patriot movement, leading to a period of open civil unrest in the 1780s. Though temporarily restored to power in 1787 by a Prussian invasion led by his brother-in-law, Frederick William II, this reliance on foreign intervention further alienated a significant portion of the Dutch populace, setting the stage for the Republic's eventual demise.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: William V's rule marked the definitive end of the Dutch Republic and the transition to a French-dominated satellite state, fundamentally altering the political landscape of the Low Countries for decades. His exile directly paved the way for the later establishment of the Kingdom of the Netherlands under his son, transforming the Orange dynasty's role.
